sections.overview: The Greylag Goose is a large, social waterfowl native across much of Europe and temperate Asia, where it uses wetlands for breeding and open grasslands or farmland for feeding. Adults are about 76–89 cm long, with a 147–180 cm wingspan and a usual mass of roughly 2.9–3.7 kg. These are wild-species measurements: released or feral domestic geese may be larger, paler, or otherwise unlike wild birds.
sections.identification: Its bulky body, thick neck and large head carry a mottled grey-brown plumage, paler breast and belly, and a white tail with a dark band; dark bars or spots on the belly vary between individuals. Pink legs and a broad bill distinguish its silhouette, while the bill colour follows geography: western European birds are usually orange-billed, eastern birds pink-billed, with intermediate birds in central Europe. In flight, large pale patches on the upperwing and a contrasting grey-and-dark underwing help identify it; the bill pattern also separates it from Taiga Bean-Goose, whose bill has dark areas and an orange band. BTO adult British means: wing length 458.8 mm and mass 3.49 kg (males), versus 436.3 mm and 3.18 kg (females). Body length is about 76–89 cm and wingspan 147–180 cm; males average larger.
sections.habitat: Breeding pairs select lakes, marshes and other wetlands with quiet nesting cover, often reedbeds or small islands that make nests less accessible to terrestrial predators. They feed in nearby meadows and wet grassland, then use larger wetlands as resting and roosting places. Outside breeding, they also graze on stubble or crops before returning to safe water; wetlands and open feeding areas therefore complement each other.
sections.diet: The Greylag is predominantly herbivorous. Its broad bill clips grasses and cereal leaves. It also digs out roots. In water, it reaches submerged plants by tipping forward. Seeds and spilled grain become important where fields are available, and the balance changes with season and locality. Its muscular gizzard helps grind fibrous plant food after it is swallowed. It may also take small aquatic animals, but plants dominate its diet.
sections.behavior: Outside nesting, families and other Greylags gather into large, noisy flocks. Honking contact calls keep birds in touch; call patterns can identify individuals and reveal social relationships. Many northern populations migrate south or west for winter, while some western and introduced populations are resident, so routes vary by population. During the annual wing moult, flight feathers are replaced together, leaving the goose unable to fly for several weeks.
sections.reproduction: Greylags are monogamous and breed in spring. British records give a typical clutch of five to seven eggs; the female incubates alone for 27–28 days. The male helps guard the goslings after hatching. The goslings hatch down-covered and precocial: once dry, they leave the nest, walk and swim, and pick up food themselves under parental protection. They fledge at about 50–60 days and commonly do not breed until around three years old.
sections.ecology: Greylags carry intact seeds in droppings between aquatic and agricultural habitats, linking plant communities across the landscape. In a long-term Dutch reedbed study, repeated grazing during the geese’s flightless moult changed reed growth and increased the movement of nitrogen and phosphorus from standing plants; this is a documented local effect, not a universal result for every marsh. Their appetite for crops can bring local conflict with farmers where flocks grow. Eggs and goslings are vulnerable to predators.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment published in 2018, based on an assessment dated 9 August 2018, classifies the Greylag Goose as Least Concern and reports an increasing overall population trend. This global result reflects the species’ very large range and population; it does not describe every local group. The same assessment identifies hunting, lead poisoning from spent shot, wetland drainage and degradation, crop conflict and disturbance or alteration of nesting habitat among pressures. In Britain, native Scottish birds coexist with re-established and naturalized populations elsewhere, so management and conflict are strongly regional. European domestic geese descend mainly from Greylags, whereas most traditional Chinese domestic geese descend from the distinct Swan Goose, Anser cygnoides; feral birds can blur the boundary between wild and managed flocks.
